claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.

A physically informed machine-learning model integrating microstructural descriptors with tensile and fracture data can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness more accurately and efficiently than conventional high-throughput methods.
Misfit volumes, elastic constants, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies are physically relevant inputs to models of alloy strengthening and ductility.
Misfit volumes, elastic constants, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies can be obtained from first-principles simulations.
Adding microstructural imaging metrics to physically derived descriptors will improve prediction of the three mechanical properties.
The training data must represent the relevant range of hierarchical microstructural states.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations in the hierarchical heterostructure mediate local elastic and plastic responses.
Misfit volumes, surface energies, and local phase-composition variations quantitatively capture the mechanical effects of the hierarchical heterostructure.
Correlating physically motivated descriptors of chemical and phase heterogeneity with measured responses can predict macroscopic mechanical properties.
Computing selected descriptors and using them in a model can bypass full-scale high-throughput DFT or CALPHAD calculations.
Elastic-property prediction can be informed by calculated moduli and elastic constants.
Fracture toughness can be predicted from fracture-related surface energies and unstable stacking-fault energies.
The hybrid model will reduce prediction error by roughly 20–30% relative to traditional CALPHAD or full first-principles calculations.
The hybrid model will reduce computational time by at least one order of magnitude.
High-throughput first-principles calculations are computationally expensive, and direct DFT evaluation of alloy yield or fracture strength is generally out of reach.
CALPHAD calculations can require significant computing resources and can have limited accuracy when reliable HEA databases are absent.
The model will become less reliable if phase separation or coarsening significantly alters the hierarchical heterostructure.
The model will become less reliable when deformation or fracture mechanisms and test conditions lie outside those represented in its training data.

contradictions.description: The predicted accuracy gain is roughly 20–30%, but the hypothesis is only falsified below a 15% gain. A blinded result between 15% and 20% would fail the stated prediction while not meeting the stated falsification rule.
